questions.q: In the Northbridge Retail case study, what specifically allowed one developer's push to silently overwrite another's unrelated change?
options: A corrupted .git folder
No branch protection on main and no pull request review before changes landed
An outdated version of the sf CLI
Too many scratch orgs being created at once
questions.explain: With no branch protection and no required PR review, changes could be pushed directly to main with nobody checking for conflicts or overlaps before they became permanent.

questions.q: What was the actual mistake in how the rushed developer resolved the package.xml conflict?
options: They ran a validation-only deploy before merging
They picked one side's <members> list entirely, discarding a teammate's legitimate addition, instead of taking the union of both
They used a merge driver instead of resolving by hand
They deleted package.xml entirely
questions.explain: The correct resolution for most package.xml conflicts, per Lesson 15, is the union of both sides' legitimate additions — picking one side and discarding the other's intended component is exactly the mistake that caused QA to find a missing field.

questions.q: Why does the remediation plan recommend moving developers to individual scratch orgs instead of a single shared sandbox?
options: Scratch orgs are required by Salesforce for any Git-tracked project
A shared sandbox lets multiple developers' changes collide in the same org at the same time, which isolated scratch orgs per feature branch prevent
Scratch orgs are cheaper than sandboxes
Scratch orgs don't require a definition file
questions.explain: Multiple developers editing one shared full sandbox simultaneously is a direct cause of changes silently colliding — per-feature scratch orgs isolate each developer's work until it's deliberately merged.

questions.q: According to this lesson's closing argument, what is the real underlying failure pattern behind incidents like Northbridge Retail's, as opposed to "the team doesn't know Git"?
options: A single catastrophic bug in the Git software itself
Several small, individually-reasonable-looking shortcuts (skipping review once, allowing a direct push once, picking a side in a conflict once) compounding over time
A lack of available training materials on Git
An intentional decision by management to avoid using branches
questions.explain: The lesson argues real teams rarely fail from not knowing basic commands — they fail when several small process shortcuts, each individually plausible in the moment, compound into a real incident.

questions.q: Given six developers and no complex multi-environment release train yet, which branching approach does the case study's remediation plan recommend for Northbridge Retail?
options: Full Git Flow with release/* and hotfix/* branches from day one
No branches at all, continuing the current approach
A lightweight trunk-based approach with short-lived feature branches merged frequently
One branch per developer that never merges into main
questions.explain: The plan recommends matching the branching model to the team's actual needs (Lesson 13) — a lightweight trunk-based approach (Lesson 14) fits a six-developer team without a heavyweight multi-environment release train yet.
